Trying to Conceive

Rheumatoid arthritis and fertility: planning treatment and pregnancy

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) does not mean that you cannot have children. Some people take longer to conceive, and disease activity, pain, age, sexual difficulties and particular medicines can all matter. The useful question is how to control your disease while making a pregnancy plan that fits the person taking each medicine.

What rheumatoid arthritis is

RA is a long-term autoimmune disease: inflammation affects the lining of joints and can also involve other organs. Painful, swollen, warm joints and stiffness after waking or resting are common; the hands and feet are often affected on both sides. Symptoms may flare and settle, and fatigue can be substantial.

Joint pain alone does not establish RA. A clinician combines the history, examination, blood tests and sometimes imaging; there is no single test that proves or excludes every case. Genetics and environmental factors contribute, while smoking and obesity are associated with risk. An injury or infection is not a proven explanation for every person's RA.

Complications deserve care, not assumptions

Uncontrolled inflammation can damage joints and affect the lungs, heart, eyes, nerves or blood vessels. Rheumatoid nodules can occur under the skin and are not necessarily painful. Bone thinning is another concern, particularly with corticosteroid exposure; some treatments increase infection risk. These are possible complications, not an inevitable course for everyone.

Dry eyes, dry mouth or vaginal dryness may reflect associated Sjögren's disease or another condition and deserve assessment. New skin ulcers, persistent cough, breathlessness, eye pain or changes in vision should be reported promptly rather than attributed automatically to a usual flare. Routine monitoring of blood counts, liver or kidney function depends on the disease and treatment.

Can RA make pregnancy take longer?

Some women with RA need more time to conceive, but a diagnosis does not establish permanent infertility. Active inflammation, age, difficulty having comfortable intercourse and medicine effects may contribute alongside unrelated ovulation, tubal or partner factors. Do not assume every irregular period is caused by RA.

A prospective study published in 2015 followed 245 women with RA and found that 42% had a time to pregnancy over 12 months. Higher disease activity and use of certain anti-inflammatory medicines or prednisone were associated with delay. This selected cohort does not give an individual's probability or prove that a medicine caused the delay; reducing treatment without an alternative can worsen disease.

Male fertility and sexual function

Men with inflammatory arthritis can also have fertility or sexual difficulties. Pain, fatigue, reduced desire, erection problems, inflammation and specific drugs may matter. A study of 628 men with several types of inflammatory arthritis found more reported fertility problems when the diagnosis occurred earlier in reproductive life. It was not a sperm study of RA alone and cannot show that every flare temporarily stops sperm production.

Sulfasalazine can reduce sperm quality reversibly in some men; a clinician may consider an alternative when conception is delayed while also investigating other causes. Cyclophosphamide, used in selected severe diseases rather than routine RA care, can cause lasting fertility damage and warrants fertility-preservation counselling before treatment. Effects on sperm production and risks to an established pregnancy are different questions.

Making intimacy more comfortable

Pain, stiffness, tiredness, dryness and concerns about your body can reduce opportunities for intercourse without meaning that eggs or sperm are absent. Discuss painful sex, persistent vaginal dryness or erection problems openly with the care team. They are treatable concerns, and partner assessment should not be postponed simply because one person has RA.

Choose times when symptoms are easier, use positions that protect sore joints and take breaks. Ask about suitable treatment for dryness and a lubricant compatible with attempts to conceive. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and psychological support can help with comfort, practical tasks and distress; none should be presented as a guaranteed fertility treatment.

Plan before stopping contraception

Arrange a joint plan with the rheumatology team and the clinician providing preconception or pregnancy care. The aim is remission or low disease activity on treatment suitable for the planned pregnancy. Several months of stable control are often helpful; the exact timing also depends on age, disease severity and the required medicine changes.

Bring the names, doses and schedules of all prescriptions, painkillers, supplements and herbal products. Review previous pregnancy outcomes, other autoimmune conditions, blood pressure, organ involvement, vaccinations and folate needs. Ask for a written plan stating who to contact if a test is positive or a flare occurs. There is no single waiting interval that applies to every RA medicine.

Disease control remains treatment, not just pain relief

Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) aim to limit inflammation and damage, while pain relief alone may not protect joints. Hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and several other treatments can be used during pregnancy when appropriate. Current EULAR guidance also allows TNF inhibitors during pregnancy after an individualized assessment; a blanket ban on all biological medicines is misleading.

The choice depends on the exact drug, dose, disease and stage of pregnancy. Sulfasalazine requires review of folic-acid supplementation. Regular NSAID use around ovulation may interfere with conception in some people, and their pregnancy restrictions require separate advice. Steroids also need a dose-and-duration plan. Do not abruptly stop prescribed steroids or replace a DMARD with an unverified supplement.

Maternal methotrexate and leflunomide need advance planning

Methotrexate used for RA must not be taken during pregnancy because it can cause pregnancy loss and fetal harm. It needs to be stopped before attempting conception with a replacement disease-control plan. EULAR discusses a 1–3 month interval, while the current US tablet label advises contraception for 6 months after the last dose. Your prescriber should reconcile the relevant product label and clinical guidance for you; these numbers are not instructions to choose your own stop date.

Leflunomide is also avoided during pregnancy. Its active metabolite may persist for up to two years without accelerated elimination. A specialist may arrange a drug-elimination procedure and blood-level confirmation before conception. Do not attempt a washout at home. Human pregnancy observations, often after early discontinuation and washout, are somewhat reassuring but do not establish that continuing leflunomide is safe.

Paternal exposure is a separate decision

A father's treatment does not expose a pregnancy in the same way as a mother's treatment during pregnancy. EULAR considers paternal low-dose methotrexate up to 25 mg weekly and paternal leflunomide compatible with conception on current evidence. This is an evidence-based specialist assessment, not a guarantee or advice to change a prescription; reassuring paternal data must not be applied to maternal use.

Some product labels remain more precautionary: the current US methotrexate label advises male contraception during treatment and for 3 months afterwards, while the leflunomide label advises stopping and elimination or blood-level verification before fathering a child. Ask the rheumatologist to document a plan that considers the local label, dose, available evidence and risk of a flare. Do not stop a well-controlled treatment without discussing an alternative.

If pregnancy happens unexpectedly

Contact the prescribing and maternity teams as soon as pregnancy is suspected or confirmed. If you are the pregnant person taking methotrexate or leflunomide, do not take another dose and seek immediate specialist advice; leflunomide may require prompt supervised elimination. Give the exact drug, dose, dates and last menstrual period. Do not wait for a routine antenatal appointment or try a home antidote.

An exposure does not by itself establish that fetal harm has occurred. Individual risk assessment and appropriate scans or other follow-up are needed. This urgent drug-specific action is different from stopping all RA treatment: many medicines can be continued, and an uncontrolled flare can also be harmful. A father's exposure requires its own assessment rather than the maternal emergency instructions.

What to expect during pregnancy

Many people with RA have successful pregnancies. Some experience symptom improvement, but others remain active or worsen; pregnancy is not a treatment or a cure. The older claim that almost everyone improves is too reassuring. Plan follow-up even when joints feel better, and keep the rheumatology and maternity teams informed about medicine changes.

Poorly controlled disease is associated with preterm birth, smaller babies and some maternal complications. RA itself has not been shown to increase birth-defect risk, but certain medicines can. Miscarriage studies are mixed, so neither a universal increased risk nor a promise of no risk is justified. Birth planning should account for joint mobility and any neck, heart or lung involvement; tell the anaesthesia team about these issues.

After birth and during breastfeeding

Symptoms can flare in the months after birth. Arrange a plan for restarting or adjusting treatment, feeding choices and practical help before delivery. Many RA treatments are compatible with breastfeeding, but each medicine needs its own assessment; pregnancy compatibility and breastfeeding compatibility are not interchangeable.

Methotrexate is not a routine breastfeeding choice: US labelling advises avoiding breastfeeding during treatment and for a week afterwards, while EULAR only conditionally considers low weekly doses when no compatible alternative can be used. Leflunomide should be avoided during breastfeeding. Ask for a documented specialist plan rather than making your own feeding interruption schedule. Tell the baby's clinician about biological treatment during pregnancy so any live-vaccine timing is individualized.

When fertility assessment is useful

Preconception medicine review should happen before trying, without waiting for an infertility threshold. If pregnancy does not occur with regular unprotected intercourse, assessment is usually advised after 12 months when the female partner is under 35, or after 6 months at 35 or older. Over 40, more immediate assessment may be appropriate.

Seek earlier assessment for irregular or absent periods, known reproductive problems, previous fertility-damaging treatment or difficulties having intercourse. Evaluate both partners together when both contribute to conception; semen analysis may be part of that work-up. A delay should lead to investigation of all plausible causes, not an automatic diagnosis of RA-related infertility or a promise that stopping one drug will solve it.

Symptoms that should not wait for a fertility visit

Get urgent medical assessment for sudden severe joint pain, new joint swelling or skin-colour change, difficulty moving a joint, or joint pain with fever or feeling hot, cold or shivery. Joint infection can occur without fever and may resemble a flare. If no emergency features are present, new or increased breathlessness also needs urgent advice, particularly during immune-suppressing treatment.

Seek emergency help immediately for severe breathing difficulty, a tight or heavy chest, pain spreading to the arms, back, neck or jaw, lips or skin turning very pale, blue or grey, or sudden confusion. These are separate warning signs; do not wait for all of them. On darker skin, colour change may be easier to see on the palms. Do not drive yourself to emergency care: arrange help or an ambulance. These symptoms are not explained safely by a fertility concern or an assumed RA flare.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask your rheumatology and preconception teams for a written medicine-by-medicine plan for the person taking each treatment, including what to do after a positive pregnancy test.

Record symptom activity, menstrual or sexual difficulties, medicine doses and dates, and how long you have been trying; bring both partners' relevant history to fertility assessment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organize symptom notes, medicine names and dates, fertility questions and planned appointments. It cannot diagnose RA-related infertility, decide a drug washout or safe conception date, predict fetal harm or replace urgent medical care.

When to seek help

Pregnant or possibly pregnant while taking methotrexate or leflunomide: do not take another dose and contact the prescribing and maternity teams immediately. Otherwise, do not stop disease-control medicines without an agreed plan. New severe joint pain, swelling, colour change or movement difficulty needs urgent assessment even without fever. Severe breathing difficulty, a tight or heavy chest, pain spreading to the arms/back/neck/jaw, very pale/blue/grey lips or skin, or sudden confusion needs emergency help; these are independent signs, and you should not drive yourself.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • RA does not mean inevitable infertility; disease activity, age, sexual function and particular medicines need separate assessment.
  • Plan stable disease control and medicine changes before conception, with both partners considered.
  • Maternal methotrexate or leflunomide exposure requires urgent specialist action; paternal recommendations are different.
  • Pregnancy may improve symptoms but does not cure RA; postpartum and breastfeeding plans matter.
  • Investigate delayed conception and urgent new symptoms rather than blaming everything on RA.

Frequently asked questions

Does rheumatoid arthritis definitely cause infertility?

No. Some people take longer to conceive, but many have children. Inflammation, age, pain, sexual difficulties, medicines and unrelated reproductive factors may all contribute. Neither guaranteed infertility nor a guarantee of unchanged fertility is accurate.

Can a man with RA become a father?

Yes. Review disease control, sexual function and medicines. Sulfasalazine can reversibly affect sperm quality in some men, while other drugs have different effects. Paternal exposure is not equivalent to maternal exposure, and a shared fertility assessment may be needed.

Should I stop all RA medicine before trying?

No. A flare can undermine health and pregnancy planning. Arrange a specific plan for each drug, including any replacement, waiting period and folate advice. Methotrexate and leflunomide require particular maternal planning; some other DMARDs and biological treatments can be continued.

What if I become pregnant while taking methotrexate or leflunomide?

If you are the pregnant person, do not take another dose and contact the prescribing and maternity teams immediately. Leflunomide may require supervised elimination. Provide doses and dates; exposure alone does not prove fetal harm. Do not use a home washout or stop every other medicine without advice.

Are methotrexate instructions the same for the father?

No. EULAR considers paternal doses up to 25 mg weekly compatible with conception, whereas the US label retains a 3-month contraception precaution after stopping. Maternal use during pregnancy remains contraindicated for RA. Ask the specialist to reconcile the applicable advice for the exact treatment.

Will pregnancy make RA disappear or guarantee a healthy baby?

No. Symptoms may improve or remain active, and flares can occur after birth. Many pregnancies go well, but disease control and medicine selection affect risk. RA itself is not known to increase birth defects; this does not make every RA medicine suitable for pregnancy.

When should we seek fertility help?

Arrange medicine planning before trying. Fertility evaluation is usually appropriate after 12 months under age 35, after 6 months at 35 or older, and sooner over 40 or with irregular periods, known reproductive risks or sexual difficulties. Both partners should be assessed when relevant.

Can a new painful joint simply be a flare?

It may be, but sudden severe pain, new swelling or colour change, difficulty moving the joint, or joint pain with fever or chills needs urgent assessment for infection. Fever may be absent. Severe breathing difficulty, a tight or heavy chest, spreading pain, very pale/blue/grey lips or skin, or sudden confusion requires emergency help; do not drive yourself or wait for all signs.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
